sequence.text: Which of the below would best describe your app? Please note that when answering questions about your app, advertising content should not be considered.

Does the game/image contain inferences of, references to, or depictions of violence, blood, or gory images? This includes violence directed at the player's character. Please note that this question does not refer to user-generated content.

content.text: Please note that this section includes all forms of violence or blood, even mild combat action or avoidance of deliberate environmental hazards.

reveals.text: Please select all that the game/image includes:

options.text: Violence or implied violence against humans

content.text: The characters must look like humans. If a character looks like a human, it should be treated as a human even if it is unrealistic. Characters that are clad in armor or obscured in some other way, but understood to be human, should also be considered human. Implied violence against humans, such as the shooting of vehicles understood to have humans inside, would also be considered violence against humans.

reveals.text: How would you describe the reactions to violence?

content.text: This refers to how reactions to violent acts are portrayed.

content.heading: Unrealistic
content.text: Characters react to violence in a way that is not representative of real life, such as by disappearing or by being so small as to obscure what is happening. The key is the reaction to violent action. If a realistically depicted character reacts to violence in an exaggerated or nonsensical way, this would still be considered an unrealistic portrayal of violence despite the fact that the character may appear "photorealistic" in depiction.

content.heading: Realistic
content.text: Depictions of violence where the character reacts as it would in real life or descriptions of violence in a real-world setting.

reveals.text: How is this violence presented in the game/image?

content.text: A violent act might be interpreted differently based on how close a player is to the action and how frequently this content occurs.

content.heading: Referred To
content.text: Some game/images might not have violence as part of the primary game/image mechanic, but instead have a storyline or plot point involving a violent act that is communicated strictly as described - not visually, but referred to via text or dialogue such as a newspaper headline referring to a murder or two characters discussing a foiled assassination plot.

content.heading: Implied
content.text: This is where players do not actually see the violence against humans, but it is obvious that it is happening. It covers such matters as the bombing of a city where players know civilians are killed or injured, blowing up a tank or shooting down a plane where players know that the crew is killed, smashing into cars or other vehicles where the driver/passenger must be injured.

content.heading: Distant
content.text: The violence is seen, but from a distant perspective. Characters shown take up a small portion of the screen. Examples of game/images that typically fall into this category are strategy game/images, platformers, and top-down shooters.

content.heading: Close-up
content.text: The violence is shown up-close, thus possessing the ability to depict detail. Characters shown take up a moderate or large portion of the screen. Examples of game/images that typically fall into this category are first- and third-person shooters or game/images that include interactive video sequences of violence.

reveals.text: What is the level of blood and/or gore associated with this violence?

content.text: This section describes how much blood and/or gore is associated with the acts of violence.

content.heading: Mild/Limited
content.text: While there is some blood, its use is constrained to very limited and purposeful uses. Examples include the following: Infrequent pools of static blood in a crime-solving game/image indicating to the player that a murder took place at that location Brief puffs of blood in a shooting game/image that indicate to the player that the target has been hit.

content.heading: Moderate
content.text: There is more blood than just the minimum required to communicate an event (such as that seen at the Mild/Limited level) or some mild dismemberment, but some restraint in the volume, frequency, and realism is still shown. Examples include the following: A shooting game/image that shows brief puffs of blood to indicate that the target was hit, and also bloodstains appear on the surface of the character and on the surface of the wall behind the target Explosions that cause characters to burst into small chunks that are somewhat distant from the viewer Frequent depictions of large bloodstains on the floor A game/image that allows the player to continue triggering blood effects on dead bodies A depiction of an impalement with limited blood

content.heading: High
content.text: Blood and/or gore are major components of the game/image. Whether by sheer volume, realism of the depiction, or intensity, the level of blood and/or gore in these game/images stands out. Examples include: A fighting game/image that allows the winner of each match to dismember the opponent A depiction of large sprays of blood after someone is slashed with a sword A scene depicting the dismemberment of a character with graphic detail

reveals.text: Can innocent or defenseless characters be seriously injured or killed?

guideline.title: Violence Towards Vulnerable or Defenseless Characters

content.text: Innocent characters are defined as bystanders that are not necessarily involved in the game/image's objective. The uninvolved characters must be visibly vulnerable to the attacks by either being permanently injured or killed. If the game/image actively encourages the killing of defenseless characters, this aspect must always be confirmed with "Yes." This also includes any mass killings of innocent characters, such as where groups of characters are killed or injured at random for no apparent reason and deals with themes such as the killing of pedestrians on the street, shoppers in a shopping arcade, or children in a school. These actions occur "without consequences" when the perpetrator is able to commit them without penalty or drawback. These actions occur "with consequences" when something negative occurs to the perpetrator (e.g., the game/image restarts after shooting a civilian, police arrest a character after the character drives through and kills a crowd of bystanders).

content.text: The setting of a game/image refers to the universe/storyline in which the action takes place.

content.heading: Fantastical
content.text: A Fantastical setting is a setting that is not substantially similar to the real world.

content.heading: Realistic
content.text: Should the action occur in a universe that is substantially similar to the real world, submitters should indicate that the setting is Realistic. There can be some fantastical elements (such as a character with super powers), but if the majority of the content in the game/image resembles the real world, it should be considered realistic.

reveals.text: Does the game/image take place in a realistic or historical war setting?

content.text: Submitters should answer "Yes" if the game/image has a realistic war setting as its main theme. This includes historic and recent as well as ongoing military or political conflicts. This question must also be confirmed for products with fictional conflicts or in which some historical facts are altered as long as the setting or storyline is rooted in real life events. Submitters should answer "No" if the game/image only references war in text or dialogue or where only a small portion of the game/imageplay takes place within a war scenario. War themes set in the distant future or in purely fictional universes without any parallels to history or present should also not be indicated here.

content.text: A childlike style is more likely to appeal to younger children. content.text: Illegal drugs are drugs that are typically illegal in most cases. Recreational drugs are drugs that are used without medical justification. The drugs must be real and not fantasy drugs.

reveals.text: Illegal or Recreational Drugs

content.text: The drugs concerned should be illegal or used recreationally. The drugs must be real and not fantasy drugs.

content.heading: Reference
content.text: Text, dialogue, lyrics, and/or images of illegal/recreational drugs would be considered references.

content.heading: Use
content.text: The use/consumption of illegal/recreational drugs in any case would constitute use.

content.heading: Encourages/Glamorizes
content.text: If characters gain advantage or achieve success (e.g., win the game/image, get the girl, kill the enemy, commit the crime) after the use of illegal/recreational drugs, this would be considered encouragement/glamorization.

reveals.text: Is the use of illegal or recreational drugs interactive?

content.text: The player's input may influence actions and/or the character can actively choose to use drugs and/or control the drug use. For example, the player can choose whether or not to light a joint or bong or control the amount of the drug to consume. A character simply touching, running into or past a depiction of a drug in a game/image would typically not satisfy this criteria.

reveals.text: Is the use of illegal or recreational drugs related to incentives or rewards?

content.text: This means the player is given a reward like a special ability (super-speed) or a more powerful weapon or can progress easier through the game/image having used the drug. A fictional storyline which may reference criminal activities or crime themes such as the drugs trade, would typically not satisfy this criteria.

Fantasy drugs are drugs that do not exist in real life but mirror the effects of real-word drugs. A fantasy drug affects characters in ways that appear similar to how real-world drugs might behave. References to modern drug terminology/slang (e.g., "getting high," "junkie," "dealer") or depictions of drug paraphernalia/accessories (e.g., vials, syringes, bongs) are usually indicators that the fantasy drugs mirror real-word drugs. Items such as healing/health potions and mushroom power-ups would not be considered fantasy drugs without these references or depictions.

sequence.text: Does the game/image natively allow users to interact or exchange content with other users through voice communication, text, or sharing images or audio?

content.text: Submitters should answer "Yes" to this question if users can freely exchange content they have created. This includes the ability to communicate between users, comment on provided content, share photos, or exchange any other type of content created by users. To help define an online interaction or content exchange, developers should only consider their game/image's native services and not consider sharing that is accomplished by using secondary apps (such as Facebook or Twitter). Please note that multiplayer functionality by itself (with no means for communication or sharing) would not require indicating "Yes" to this question.

sequence.text: Does the game/image share the user's current and precise physical location with other users?

content.text: Submitters should answer "Yes" only if the game/image transmits the user's current, precise location to other people. Broad location information (e.g, "New York City," "Germany," "Leicester Square") is not specific enough to be considered precise. Essentially, if players of the game/image could find each other in the real world based on information provided by the game/image, then this question should be marked "Yes." This includes game/images that share users' locations within the game/image itself (e.g., a game/image that displays the location of all users of the game/image on a real-world map) or broadcast users' location data to other apps (e.g., a game/image posting your location to a social network). Submitters should not say "Yes" if the game/image merely uses the users' location but does not share it with others. Examples of functions that would not trigger a "Yes" to this question would be accessing a user's location to provide ideal server selections or using a user's location to select a default language for the game/image.

sequence.text: Does the game/image advocate committing acts of terrorism?

content.text: This means your game/image advocates or praises the doing of a terrorist act in the real world or provides instruction on how to commit terrorism. Note: there is a high threshold for this content and it would not typically include game/images clearly for entertainment where the player must stop or fight terrorists or where fictional "terrorist" characters form part of the game/image's fictional plot or theme.

sequence.text: Does the game/image contain any swastikas, other Nazi symbols or propaganda deemed unconstitutional in Germany?

content.text: Submitters should check "YES" if any of the following are included: The swastika as used by the Nazi regime, the SS-rune found on uniform badges and insignia from the "Waffen-SS", the salute "Heil Hitler", the accompanying "Hitlergruß" (arm gesture), original portraits or busts of Adolf Hitler in a glorifying manner and songs used for Nazi propaganda in WW2 ("Horst-Wessel-Lied"). See Example 1. Submitters should check "NO" when using the "Iron Cross", the "Reichskriegsflagge" without swastika or the general display or mentioning of Adolf Hitler or the Nazi regime in a non-glorifying context. The deciding aspect is the lack of any positive connotation. See Example 2.

sequence.text: Does the game/image contain any content that can substantially erode the national identity of the Republic of Korea by describing anti-national acts or distorting historical facts?
Does the game/image contain realistic descriptions of crimes (e.g., robbery, kidnapping) or techniques that can be used in criminal offenses?

reveals.text: Are these crimes or criminal techniques likely to be imitated by children or youths?
Are there detailed descriptions of techniques that could be used in criminal offenses?

content.text: This means your game/image gives very detailed and very specific information and instruction to players and, based on the contents of your game/image alone, players could commit a crime in the real-world. For example a step-by-step instruction manual showing how to make a Molotov cocktail or bomb would be included under this question as would details of the implements needed to break into a car and how to use them. Note that game/images where the player controls a fictional criminal character as part of the game/image's fictional plot or crime-theme would typically not satisfy this requirement.
